Peak Poker Performance

   I’m going to reveal the answers to these questions in this chapter, and I
hope you’ll be pleasantly surprised. As poker players, the only “tool” of the
trade we have is our mind. How well you focus, and how fast you are at
making decisions and solving complex puzzles all come down to how effi-
ciently your brain operates.
   The basic biology is this: the human brain shrinks and cognitive per-
formance declines with age. Did you know that after the age of 30, your
IQ will decrease by 5% each decade unless you take action to prevent it?
Even if you are still in your 20s, it’s unlikely that you have optimized your
brain to such a degree that it is operating at full capacity. You can make
certain choices that will virtually guarantee that your brain operates at a
markedly higher level, and you can put a halt to the brain shrinkage that
occurs with age. If you want to tap the full potential of your brain, this
chapter is for you.
   One of the most exciting discoveries in recent years has revealed that
the parts of the brain involved in memory, attention, and problem solving
have an innate ability to grow and change. This process is called plasticity.
While these areas can also shrink if you make poor choices, they can be-
come thicker, denser, and larger in response to good choices. What we
now know is that the brain can grow at any age, and it can do so within
weeks of making certain lifestyle changes.
   After reading the previous chapter, you have a much better idea of
your brain’s physiology and how the various parts work together. The
purpose of this chapter is to show practical strategies you can use to
boost your cognitive performance. Everything you do is a reflection of the
brain you currently have. How well you respond to three bets and put
people on hand ranges, and how quickly you calculate pot-odds is a direct
reflection of your brain’s size and health. Are you able to arrive at deci-
sions quickly or do you sometimes feel tired, sluggish, and fuzzy?
   If you are on the sluggish side, be reassured that there are steps you
can take to improve your brain’s growth and function. Brain growth, or
plasticity, occurs across all areas of the brain in the form of newly born
synapses (when you learn something new), larger and more intricate

Brain Booster #1: Exercise
Neuroscientist Fred Gage was the first to show that exercise alone could
increase the number of neurons being born in the hippocampus (the part
of the brain responsible for memory). Initial studies were done with rats,
but today there’s plenty of evidence that shows that what’s good for the
lab rat is good for the human. Kirk Erickson is currently one of the leading
researchers in this area. He has conducted multiple studies that show
regular exercisers have more volume in the hippocampus, which helps
them to perform better on tests of memory.
    Brain-derived neurotrophic factor is probably the major reason for such
improvements. You want a lot of brain-derived neurotrophic factor be-
cause it prevents the death of existing brain cells and encourages the
growth of new neurons and synapses. Exercise really gets the brain-
derived neurotrophic factor pumping, and is like Miracle-Gro for your brain.
The younger you are when you start exercising regularly, the better, but
research shows it is never too late. Older people who start exercising regu-
larly stop brain shrinkage and actually show brain growth. Erickson also

Peak Poker Performance

found that regular exercise increases gray matter in the frontal lobes.
That’s the part of your brain that powers high level thinking, planning and
analyzing, and regulates willpower. Whether you are calculating odds or
simply waiting patiently for hands, you are using your frontal lobes.
   Another reason exercise is so powerful is because it gets your blood
and oxygen pumping. When you exercise, you increase the number of
blood vessels in your brain (a process called angiogenesis). The more
blood vessels you have, the more nourishment your brain receives, and
the faster and more efficiently it operates.
   Finally, exercise has been shown to increase alpha brain waves. Alpha
waves are associated with a calm, alert, focused state of mind. Harvard
psychiatrist John Ratey says exercise is like a little bit of Prozac (an anti-
depressant) and a little bit of Ritalin (a stimulant used to treat ADHD).
There are studies that show exercise is just as effective as anti-depressant
medication for mild to moderate depression. Similar results have also been
found for patients who suffer from mild to moderate ADHD. To think more
clearly and increase your focus, exercise is the way to go.
   The question up for debate now is how much exercise it takes to pro-
mote brain health, and what kinds of exercise are best. Research suggests
that vigorous aerobic activity is the best. There are studies showing that
high-intensity interval training along with resistance training offers cogni-
tive benefits. It’s best to start slowly and work your way up to five days a
week. The most important advice is to do the activities you find fun. Ex-
ercise is easiest to stick with if you pick activities you like. Things like bas-
ketball, tennis, rowing, or swimming can all be good brain builders. Just
make sure to check with your physician before you start an exercise pro-
gram. Once you get an all clear, make exercise a keystone habit. It will
help your brain in a multitude of ways!

Brain Booster #3: Mindfulness Meditation
To begin to understand why meditation is so beneficial to the brain it’s
helpful to know something about how neurons communicate. Your brain
transmits information using a neurochemical-electrical process that pro-
duces brain waves, which can be measured using a tool called an electro-
encephelagram (EEG). There are several patterns of brain waves:

   ♠ delta waves (1–3 hertz): associated with deep sleep; very slow
       waves
   ♠ theta waves (4–7 hertz): associated with drowsiness or brain
       injuries that lead to slow waves
   ♠ alpha waves (8–12 hertz): associated with calm, focused,
       alertness; mid-range waves that are ideal for playing poker in an
       optimum state
   ♠ beta waves (greater than 12 hertz): associated with heightened
       awareness and problem solving; excessive amounts of beta waves
       are correlated with anxiety and insomnia

                    Enhance Your Brain’s Performance: Brain Boosters

    Neuroscientists have learned that a racing brain is not necessarily a
healthy one. The ideal state for your brain to be in most of the time is the
alpha state. Recent studies have shown that you can train your brain to be
in this state more often, and the primary way to do this is through medita-
tion.
    “Meditation” is a broad term that describes the use of deliberate tech-
niques to induce a state of relaxation, attentional focus, and contemplation.
It could involve repeating certain words or phrases, regulating your breath-
ing, or directing your thoughts in a particular way. There are many types of
meditative practices and all have been shown to benefit the brain.
    When you meditate (or engage in other types of mindful contempla-
tion, like yoga or tai chi), your goal is to train your state of consciousness
in such a way that it benefits you. Typically, the perks of a meditation
practice include relaxation, stress reduction, heightened awareness, and
improved concentration. Meditation is not just a relaxation agent, though.
It reduces spiky beta waves (which are bad in excess), increases the size
of the hippocampus, boosts brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and im-
proves oxygen flow. Besides all these benefits, regular meditation im-
proves sleep, boosts the immune system, and improves blood pressure.
Several small studies have shown that the size of several areas of the
brain, including the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex, increases in
people who meditate. Increases in those areas, in particular, correlate
with improved memory and better self-discipline.
    While more research is needed to more fully understand how medita-
tion impacts the brain, it is safe to say that meditation is a key brain
booster. Besides all of these wonderful benefits, meditation is also very
powerful in improving attention and emotional regulation. Dr. Richard
Davidson has done a number of imaging studies on meditators that show
meditation is associated with increased activity in the parts of the brain
responsible for paying attention. His studies also show that there is a link
between meditation and the ability to process information more quickly. It
appears that regular meditation can help you think more efficiently and
rapidly.

Peak Poker Performance

    It has also been reported that meditation positively affects the brain’s
underlying patterns that produce anxiety, stress, depression, and irritabil-
ity, so when they arise they dissipate more quickly and easily. On average,
meditators rate themselves as happier and more contented than before
they meditated.
    Here’s a quick meditation that you can try whenever you’d like a brain
boost:

   ♠ Sit up straight in your chair so that your spine feels well supported.
       Keep your feet flat on the floor, and either close your eyes or just
       soften your gaze while you look at the floor.
   ♠ Focus your attention on your breath as it flows in and out of your
       nostrils. Observe the sensations you feel as the air flows in and out
       of your nose. There is no need to alter your breath in any way; just
       observe it without looking for anything in particular to happen.
   ♠ After a bit, you’ll probably notice that your mind starts to wander.
       When you notice this, just bring your attention back to your
       breathing without criticizing yourself. The act of noticing that your
       attention has wandered and bringing it back is the key component
       of practicing meditation. Do this for a total of one minute.
   ♠ You may notice that your mind becomes very calm during this
       minute. Or you may experience all sorts of thoughts (the so called
       monkey mind). Either is perfectly fine and natural. Note that the
       thoughts and feelings that arise from them are very fleeting.
   ♠ Once the one minute is up, you may open your eyes and re-orient
       to the room.

   That’s all there is to getting started with meditation. It is a very pow-
erful practice, and I hope that you will add it to your daily routine. People
tend to see significant improvements within just a few weeks of starting a
meditation practice.

                    Enhance Your Brain’s Performance: Brain Boosters

Brain Booster #4: Proper Sleep
The National Institutes of Health reports that as many as 40 million
Americans suffer from chronic sleep disorders each year, while another
20 million occasionally suffer from sleep disorders. Poor sleep over pro-
longed periods damages the brain more than you can imagine. The real
danger is that it’s usually the first thing people give up, when they want
to add more activities to their schedules. You are about to see why this is
a huge mistake!
    The major reason we need sleep is because that’s when the brain reju-
venates itself. It is during sleep that all of our brain maintenance happens.
While we sleep learning is consolidated, metabolic waste is removed, and
certain repairs are made. The important question is how much sleep is op-
timal?
    Not getting enough sleep is one of the biggest contributors to a lack-
luster performance. Being tired can make us irritable, foggy, and even
slow to react. Prolonged periods of poor sleep are known as insomnia, and
they are associated with brain shrinkage in the hippocampus and prefron-
tal cortex! As you will recall from the previous chapter, the hippocampus
is important to learning and memory, and the prefrontal cortex is where
things like self-control, planning, and decision making occur. Poor sleep
can damage your brain!
    K. Anders Ericsson is well known for discovering the 10,000 hour rule
for expert performance, which we discussed at length in Positive Poker. In
his studies of peak performers he learned something about the value of
sleep. On average, peak performers sleep a whole lot longer than average
performers. He found that they clocked in close to nine hours of sleep per
night. Compare this with the average amount of sleep people in America
get, which is only 6.8 hours per night. That’s a vast difference.
    Different people need dramatically different amounts of sleep, but
most experts suggest that people should have 7–8½ uninterrupted hours
of sleep each night. Healthy sleep patterns follow a particular structure,
where we cycle through periods of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) fol-
lowed by rapid eye movement (REM). If you are sleeping well, about 75%
